title: Executive Leadership Intensive
blurb: Three days onsite for directors and VPs, followed by 90 days of executive coaching. Strategy, influence, and leading leaders in the AI era.

modules.t: Day 1A — Strategy: Diagnosis, Choices & Coherent Action
modules.d: What strategy actually is, how to recognise bad strategy, and how to articulate yours in one page.
modules.body:
Most "strategies" are not strategies

Executives are surrounded by documents called strategy that are really goals, slogans, budgets or lists of initiatives. Richard Rumelt, in Good Strategy / Bad Strategy, identifies the hallmarks of bad strategy: fluff (impressive language with little meaning), failure to face the challenge (no clear diagnosis of what is hard), mistaking goals for strategy ("grow revenue 20%" is a desire, not a way), and bad strategic objectives (long lists of unprioritised initiatives). A strategy that does not tell people what not to do is not doing its job.

The kernel of good strategy

Rumelt's kernel has three parts. A diagnosis names the critical challenge — what makes this situation difficult and where the leverage lies. A guiding policy is the overall approach to overcoming that challenge, ruling out many options. Coherent actions are coordinated steps — resource commitments, policies, initiatives — that reinforce one another to carry out the guiding policy. The diagnosis is usually where executives under-invest: if the challenge is wrongly framed, excellent execution solves the wrong problem.

Example. A regional training institute faces declining enrolment. Goal-as-strategy: "Increase enrolment 30%." Kernel: Diagnosis — employers no longer value our generic certificates; graduates cannot show applied skill. Guiding policy — become the provider whose graduates demonstrably do the work, by partnering with employers on applied, assessed programmes. Coherent actions — co-design three programmes with employers; replace written exams with portfolio assessment; retire five low-demand courses to fund the redesign; publish placement outcomes.

Strategy as a set of choices

A. G. Lafley and Roger Martin's Playing to Win frames strategy as five integrated choices: What is our winning aspiration? Where will we play? How will we win? What capabilities must be in place? What management systems are required? "Where to play" and "how to win" are the heart: which customers, geographies, channels and offerings, and what distinctive advantage — cost leadership or differentiation — will make you win there. Choices must be mutually reinforcing; an aspiration to be premium with a cost-cutting capability system will fail.

Analysing the environment without drowning in it

Executives use frameworks to sharpen the diagnosis, not to fill slides. PESTLE scans political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental forces. Porter's five forces examines industry attractiveness: rivalry, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, buyer power and supplier power. Capability analysis asks which of your resources are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and organised to exploit (the VRIO test). The insight comes from asking "So what does this mean for our choices?" after each analysis.

Portfolio prioritisation

Most organisations attempt too many initiatives at once, starving each of the attention and talent it needs. Executive prioritisation involves explicitly ranking initiatives against strategic fit, value, risk and capacity, then stopping lower-ranked ones — the hardest and most valuable leadership act. A useful discipline: no new strategic initiative is approved without naming what will be stopped or slowed to make room.

Articulating strategy so people can act on it

If managers two levels below you cannot explain the strategy and how their work fits, it does not exist in practice. A one-page strategy should state the aspiration, the diagnosis, the where-to-play and how-to-win choices, the three to five priority actions, what you will stop, and the measures of progress. Then repeat it — leaders consistently underestimate how often strategy must be communicated before it is understood and used.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my strategy sparring partner. I will describe my organisation's situation. First, push me for a sharper diagnosis of the critical challenge. Then help me write Rumelt's kernel (diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions) and the five Playing to Win choices. Finally, identify which current initiatives contradict the strategy and should be stopped, and draft a one-page strategy.

📚 Glossary

  • Kernel: diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent actions
  • Bad strategy: fluff, unfaced challenges, goals posing as strategy, or unprioritised objectives
  • Where to play / how to win: the core strategic choices of arena and advantage
  • VRIO: valuable, rare, inimitable, organised — tests for sustained advantage
  • Portfolio prioritisation: ranking and stopping initiatives to focus capacity

📖 References

  • Rumelt, R. (2011). Good Strategy / Bad Strategy.
  • Lafley, A. G. & Martin, R. (2013). Playing to Win.
  • Porter, M. (1979/2008). The five competitive forces that shape strategy. Harvard Business Review.
  • Barney, J. (1991). Firm resources and sustained competitive advantage. Journal of Management.

quiz.q: The board of a Douala logistics firm approves a document titled 'Strategy 2027' whose core line is 'Grow revenue 25% and become the most admired operator in Central Africa'. Using Rumelt, what is the main weakness?
opts: It sets a goal and aspiration but names no diagnosis of what makes growth hard or how to overcome it
It aims too high; a credible strategy would anchor the growth target to the industry's 8% average
It sets an ambitious target without a balanced scorecard to cascade the number to each department
It lacks a PESTLE scan of regional political and economic forces to justify the 25% revenue target
quiz.x: Rumelt calls goals posing as strategy 'bad strategy': there is no diagnosis, guiding policy or coherent actions. A PESTLE scan (runner-up) could inform a diagnosis but adding analysis does not turn a goal into a strategy.

quiz.q: A Kenyan private university's diagnosis reads: 'Employers doubt our graduates can do applied work.' The team proposes a guiding policy. Which one best fits Rumelt's kernel?
opts: Increase marketing spend to rebuild employer awareness of the quality of our existing degree programmes
Launch twelve new initiatives across teaching, research and outreach so no opportunity is missed
Raise student intake by 20% so that higher scale funds better facilities across all faculties
Become the provider whose alumni visibly do the job, via programmes co-designed and assessed with industry
quiz.x: A guiding policy is an approach that addresses the diagnosed challenge and rules options out. Marketing the existing degrees (runner-up) treats the problem as awareness when the diagnosis says the skill evidence itself is missing.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian bank's strategy states 'premium, high-touch service for corporate clients' while its capability plan centres on closing branches and cutting relationship managers by 40%. In Playing to Win terms, what is wrong?
opts: The where-to-play choice is too narrow, since retail clients offer more volume than corporate ones
The how-to-win choice and the capability choices contradict each other instead of reinforcing
The management systems are missing, so the bank cannot measure progress on the premium aspiration
The aspiration is not quantified, so staff cannot tell whether the premium service is succeeding
quiz.x: Lafley and Martin stress that the five choices must reinforce each other; a premium differentiation play with a cost-cutting capability system will fail. Missing management systems is a real gap but secondary to the contradiction.

quiz.q: An executive team in Atlanta has 23 active strategic initiatives and complains that none gets enough talent. The CEO wants one rule that changes behaviour from next quarter. Which rule does the module recommend?
opts: Ask every initiative owner to submit a monthly status report so slow projects can be spotted early
Freeze the budget of the bottom five initiatives for six months while keeping their teams in place
Require that no new initiative is approved without naming what will be stopped or slowed to make room
Rank all 23 initiatives by expected value and fund them in that order until the annual budget runs out
quiz.x: The module's discipline is 'nothing new without naming what stops'. Ranking by value (runner-up) is part of prioritisation, but without explicitly stopping work the organisation keeps starving initiatives of attention and talent.

quiz.q: A cement producer in Nigeria runs Porter's five forces and finds three major importers, falling tariffs and customers who can switch suppliers at no cost. What is the most useful next step?
opts: Commission a PESTLE scan to confirm whether the tariff trend will persist over the next five years
Ask 'so what for our choices?' — for example, which segments to serve where buyer power is lower
Add a VRIO analysis of plant capabilities so that the strategy slide deck covers both outside and inside
Present the five-forces chart to the board as evidence that the industry is in structural decline
quiz.x: The module says insight comes from asking what each analysis means for choices. More analysis (VRIO or PESTLE) may help later, but piling up frameworks without translating them into choices is 'filling slides'.

quiz.q: A Ghanaian fintech claims its advantage is a customer database of 2 million users. Competitors could build similar lists within 18 months by partnering with telcos. Under VRIO, the database is best described as:
opts: Valuable and rare today but imitable, so it gives only a temporary advantage rather than a sustained one
Not valuable, because any asset that competitors can eventually replicate has no strategic worth at all
A sustained advantage as long as the firm is organised to exploit it through a dedicated data team
A sustained competitive advantage, because 2 million users is a large and valuable base in that market
quiz.x: VRIO requires an asset to be valuable, rare, hard to imitate and organised for sustained advantage. Being organised (runner-up) does not fix imitability; an asset copied in 18 months gives temporary parity at best.

quiz.q: A regional NGO director writes a one-page strategy with aspiration, diagnosis, where-to-play and how-to-win choices, and five priority actions. A colleague says it is incomplete. Which missing element does the module emphasise?
opts: A full SWOT appendix so that donors can check the analysis behind each of the five priority actions
A detailed annual budget showing the cost of each priority action down to the line-item level
Testimonials from beneficiaries to make the strategy memorable for staff at every field office
What the NGO will stop doing, and the measures that will show whether the strategy is progressing
quiz.x: The module's one-page strategy includes what you will stop and the measures of progress. A budget (runner-up) supports execution but the module singles out 'stop' items and measures as essential to a usable strategy.

quiz.q: Six months after launch, managers two levels below a Yaoundé CEO cannot explain the strategy. The CEO presented it once at a retreat with a polished deck. According to the module, what is the most likely cause?
opts: The retreat format excluded middle managers, so the strategy should have been co-designed by them
Managers lack the analytical training needed to interpret frameworks such as the five forces
The strategy was communicated far too few times for it to be understood and used in daily work
The deck was too visual; strategy is understood better when written up as a long narrative memo
quiz.x: Leaders consistently underestimate how often strategy must be repeated before people can act on it. Co-design (runner-up) can build ownership, but the module's stated failure here is insufficient repetition.

quiz.q: Two strategy drafts for a Lagos hospital group: Draft A lists 15 initiatives all marked 'high priority'. Draft B names one diagnosis, one guiding policy and four actions that fund each other. Which statement is most accurate?
opts: Draft A is safer, because a broad list keeps more options open if conditions change unexpectedly
Draft B is better because it forces choices and its actions reinforce one another to carry out the policy
Draft A is better for a large group, since four actions are too few to engage every hospital unit
Both are acceptable, provided each initiative in Draft A is later linked to a key performance indicator
quiz.x: Rumelt lists long unprioritised objectives as a hallmark of bad strategy; coherent, mutually reinforcing actions are the kernel. Adding KPIs to Draft A (runner-up) measures the list but does not create focus.

quiz.q: A training institute's revenue fell 18%. The CEO says the diagnosis is 'weak sales effort' and doubles the sales team. A year later revenue is still falling. The most likely strategic lesson is:
opts: The guiding policy was right but the coherent actions were too few to show measurable results yet
Sales hires take two years to become productive, so the plan simply needed more patience to work
A wrongly framed diagnosis means even excellent execution solves the wrong problem
The CEO should have used a balanced scorecard to track sales activity more closely each month
quiz.x: Diagnosis is where executives under-invest; if employers no longer value the product, more selling cannot fix it. The 'too few actions' option assumes the policy was right, which the evidence does not support.

facts.t: Rumelt's kernel: diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions.
facts.more: Diagnosis is where executives under-invest — a wrongly framed challenge means excellent execution of the wrong thing.

facts.t: Playing to Win: aspiration, where to play, how to win, capabilities, systems.
facts.more: ‘Where to play’ and ‘how to win’ are the heart; all five must reinforce each other.

facts.t: Rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power, supplier power.
facts.more: Porter's lens on industry attractiveness. The value is the ‘so what for our choices?’ question after it, not the slide.

facts.t: Valuable, rare, inimitable, organised — the test for lasting advantage.
facts.more: A capability that fails any one test can be copied or wasted. Barney's resource-based view underpins it.

modules.d: Making high-stakes decisions under uncertainty, defeating bias, and using AI as a challenger.
modules.body:
Judge decisions by their quality, not just their outcomes

Annie Duke calls the habit of judging decisions by their results "resulting". Good decisions sometimes lead to bad outcomes because of luck; bad decisions sometimes lead to good ones. Executives who evaluate only outcomes learn the wrong lessons — punishing sound bets that were unlucky and rewarding reckless ones that worked. Decision quality asks: Was the frame right? Were real alternatives considered? Was relevant information sought at reasonable cost? Were values and trade-offs explicit? Was the reasoning sound? Was there commitment to action?

One-way and two-way doors

Jeff Bezos distinguished Type 1 decisions — consequential and hard to reverse, "one-way doors" — from Type 2 decisions — reversible "two-way doors". Type 1 decisions deserve deliberation, broad input and careful analysis. Type 2 decisions should be made quickly by small groups or individuals, because the cost of delay exceeds the cost of a reversible mistake. A common executive failure is applying heavy Type 1 process to every decision, which slows the organisation and centralises decisions that should be delegated.

The biases that distort executive judgement

  • Confirmation bias — seeking evidence that supports the preferred option.
  • Overconfidence — estimate ranges that are far too narrow; plans assume best cases.
  • Planning fallacy — systematically underestimating time and cost.
  • Sunk-cost fallacy — continuing because of what has already been invested.
  • Anchoring — over-relying on the first number heard.
  • Groupthink — cohesive teams suppressing dissent to maintain harmony.
  • Escalation of commitment — doubling down on a failing course to justify past choices.

Knowing about biases does little to reduce them individually; what works is process that builds in correction.

Process tools that improve decisions

The pre-mortem (Gary Klein): imagine it is a year from now and the decision has failed badly; each person writes down why. This legitimises dissent and surfaces risks that optimism hides. The outside view / reference-class forecasting (Kahneman and Flyvbjerg): instead of building estimates from your own plan, start with the actual outcomes of similar projects — how long and how much they really took — then adjust. Devil's advocate and red teams: assign someone explicitly to attack the preferred option. Multiple options: insisting on at least three genuine alternatives reduces narrow framing ("whether or not" decisions). Decision journals: record the reasoning, expectations and confidence at the time, so later review evaluates the decision, not the luck.

Expected value and scenarios. For major choices, build three to four plausible futures and estimate outcomes under each. Ask which option performs acceptably across all scenarios (robustness), not only which is best in the most likely one. Expected value helps, but for Type 1 decisions also ask: can we survive the worst case?

Using AI as a challenger, not an oracle

Generative AI is a powerful decision aid when used as a challenger: generating alternatives you missed, arguing the opposing case, running structured scenario analysis, drafting the pre-mortem, or stress-testing assumptions. Its risks are real: plausible but false facts, sycophancy toward the framing you give it, and hidden assumptions. Good practice: ask it explicitly to argue against your preferred option, verify every factual claim that matters, and keep accountability human. Never let a fluent answer substitute for evidence.

Who decides: decision rights

Many executive decision problems are really unclear decision rights. Frameworks such as RAPID (Recommend, Agree, Perform, Input, Decide) or a RACI matrix clarify who decides, who must agree, and who provides input. Ambiguity produces either paralysis or conflict; clarity allows speed.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my executive decision red team. My decision: [describe]. Step 1: classify it as a one-way or two-way door and say what process it deserves. Step 2: generate at least two genuine alternatives I have not considered. Step 3: run a pre-mortem listing the five most likely reasons it fails. Step 4: give me an outside-view base rate from similar decisions. Step 5: argue forcefully against my preferred option. Flag any facts I must verify.

📚 Glossary

  • Resulting: judging a decision by its outcome rather than its quality
  • One-way / two-way door: irreversible versus reversible decisions
  • Pre-mortem: imagining failure in advance to surface risks
  • Reference-class forecasting: estimating from outcomes of similar past cases
  • RAPID: framework clarifying decision roles

📖 References

  • Duke, A. (2018). Thinking in Bets.
  • Kahneman, D. (2011). Thinking, Fast and Slow.
  • Klein, G. (2007). Performing a project premortem. Harvard Business Review.
  • Flyvbjerg, B. & Gardner, D. (2023). How Big Things Get Done.
  • Bezos, J. (2016). Letter to Amazon shareholders.
  • Rogers, P. & Blenko, M. (2006). Who has the D? Harvard Business Review.

quiz.q: A CFO in Abidjan approved a well-researched currency hedge that lost money when the exchange rate moved unexpectedly. The board wants to discipline her. Applying Annie Duke, what should the board do first?
opts: Review the decision quality: frame, alternatives, information and reasoning at the time it was made
Discipline her, since the outcome shows the hedge was a poor decision regardless of the analysis
Compare her result with peer firms' hedges this year to see whether others lost more or less money
Ban currency hedging for two years until the board can be sure exchange rate risk is under control
quiz.x: Judging by outcome alone is 'resulting'. Peer comparison (runner-up) still judges results; the board should examine whether the process and reasoning were sound when she decided.

quiz.q: A US retailer's VP must choose between (A) testing a new checkout page on 5% of traffic, reversible in a day, and (B) signing a 15-year lease for a flagship store. How should process differ?
opts: A needs a pre-mortem and three alternatives, while B can rely on the property broker's recommendation
Both deserve the same full committee review, because consistency of process builds organisational trust
B should be delegated to the property team, while A needs CEO review since customers see the change
A should be decided quickly by a small team; B deserves deliberation, broad input and careful analysis
quiz.x: The A/B test is a two-way door: delay costs more than a reversible mistake. The lease is a one-way door. Applying the same heavy process to both (runner-up) slows the organisation and centralises decisions.

quiz.q: A Ugandan ministry estimates a new hospital will take 24 months because its own plan adds up that way. Similar hospitals in the region took 38 to 50 months. Using reference-class forecasting, what should the ministry do?
opts: Keep 24 months, since this project's plan is more detailed than those earlier, less organised projects
Add a standard 10% contingency to the 24-month plan to cover the usual optimism in schedules
Average its 24 months with the regional figures, giving about 34 months, and publish that estimate
Start from the 38–50 month range of similar projects, then adjust for specific known differences
quiz.x: The outside view starts from actual outcomes of similar projects and then adjusts. Averaging (runner-up) still anchors on the inside-view plan, and a 10% buffer is far smaller than the observed gap.

quiz.q: Before approving a 2 billion CFA ERP rollout, a CEO asks the team to imagine it is a year later and the project has failed badly, and to write down why. What is the main benefit of this exercise?
opts: It legitimises dissent and surfaces risks that the team's optimism would otherwise keep hidden
It replaces the need for a formal risk register because all risks are now identified by the team
It ensures the team commits publicly to the project, which reduces later resistance to the change
It produces a probability-weighted cost forecast that can be compared directly with the budget
quiz.x: Klein's pre-mortem makes it safe to voice doubts and reveals hidden risks. It does not replace a risk register or produce probabilities; it feeds them.

quiz.q: A Johannesburg firm has spent R40 million on a failing software project. The sponsor argues: 'We've invested too much to stop now.' Which bias is this, and what question should replace it?
opts: Groupthink; ask an outside consultant to collect anonymous opinions from the project team members
Planning fallacy; ask how long similar projects took before agreeing a revised completion date
Sunk-cost fallacy; ask whether, starting today, the remaining spend is worth the expected benefit
Anchoring; ask what the original R40 million budget estimate was based on before deciding anything
quiz.x: Past spending is sunk; the decision should rest on future costs and benefits. The planning fallacy is related (it likely caused the overrun) but does not describe the 'invested too much to stop' reasoning.

quiz.q: An executive team in Nairobi frames its decision as 'Should we open a Kampala branch or not?' A board member objects to the framing. Which improvement does the module recommend?
opts: Gather two more months of market data before deciding, to reduce uncertainty about Kampala demand
Generate at least three genuine alternatives, such as a partner model or a digital-first entry
Calculate the expected value of opening the branch under the most likely market scenario
Assign a devil's advocate to argue against opening the branch during the next executive meeting
quiz.x: Whether-or-not framing is narrow; insisting on three real alternatives widens it. A devil's advocate (runner-up) tests the preferred option but still leaves only two choices on the table.

quiz.q: Option A yields a 70% chance of +500 million and 30% chance of −300 million. Option B yields 100% chance of +200 million. The firm's cash reserve is 250 million. Which reasoning best reflects the module?
opts: Choose A, because its expected value of 260 million is higher than B's certain 200 million
A has the higher expected value (260 vs 200), but its worst case could exceed reserves, so B may be wiser
Choose B, because any option with a chance of loss should be rejected for an irreversible decision
Choose A, because over many decisions expected value wins and the 30% loss is a one-off event
quiz.x: EV(A)=0.7×500−0.3×300=260. The module says for Type 1 decisions also ask whether you can survive the worst case; a 300 million loss exceeds the 250 million reserve. Choosing A on EV alone is the runner-up trap.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian director asks an AI assistant: 'Confirm that expanding to Gabon is a strong move given our success at home.' The AI produces a fluent, supportive analysis. What is the main risk?
opts: The analysis is supportive, so it should now be shared with the board as independent validation
The AI's analysis may be too cautious, since language models tend to understate growth opportunities
The prompt invites sycophancy, so the AI may echo the framing and include unverified claims
The AI cannot handle regional data, so its view on Gabon is unusable for an executive decision
quiz.x: The module warns of sycophancy toward the given framing and plausible but false facts. Good practice is to ask the AI to argue against the preferred option and verify key claims.

quiz.q: At a Ghanaian cocoa exporter, every major purchase stalls for weeks because finance, operations and the MD each believe they have the final say. What is the most fitting diagnosis and fix?
opts: Unclear decision rights; use RAPID or RACI to specify who recommends, agrees, inputs and decides
A communication problem; hold a weekly all-hands meeting so everyone hears the same information
A bias problem; run a pre-mortem on each purchase so disagreements surface before the meeting
A capability problem; train managers on expected value so their analyses converge more quickly
quiz.x: Ambiguous decision rights produce paralysis or conflict. A pre-mortem (runner-up) improves a decision's quality but does not settle who holds the D.

quiz.q: A CEO keeps a decision journal. Eighteen months later, a launch she rated '60% likely to succeed' has failed. How should she use the journal entry?
opts: Raise her confidence threshold to 80% for all future launches so that failures become much less likely overall
Conclude her judgement was poor, since a 60% confidence rating should have produced a success
Delete the entry, because the journal is meant to record lessons from decisions that succeeded
Check whether her reasoning and information were sound, recognising a 40% failure was anticipated
quiz.x: Journals let you evaluate the decision rather than the luck; a 60% bet fails 40% of the time. Raising a threshold (runner-up) reacts to one outcome instead of examining the reasoning.

facts.t: Large projects delivering on budget, on time AND the promised benefits.
facts.more: In Flyvbjerg's database of 16,000+ projects; only 8.5% hit both cost and schedule. That is why the outside view matters.

facts.t: One-way doors vs two-way doors.
facts.more: Irreversible decisions deserve deliberation; reversible ones should be made fast and low in the organisation.

facts.t: RAPID: Recommend, Agree, Perform, Input, Decide.
facts.more: Many ‘decision problems’ are really unclear decision rights — the result is paralysis or conflict.

facts.t: Judging a decision by its outcome instead of its quality.
facts.more: Annie Duke's term. Decision journals record reasoning at the time so reviews judge the decision, not the luck.

labs.title: One-way or two-way door?
labs.intro: Classify each decision to decide how much process it deserves.
items: Closing the Garoua branch and selling the building
Signing a 10-year exclusive distribution contract
Acquiring a competitor
Choosing the CEO's successor
Testing a new email subject line
Piloting a new meeting format for one quarter

plaibox.title: Expected value & survival check
plaibox.intro: A one-way-door investment. Compare expected value with whether you can survive the worst case.

inputs.label: Net gain if it succeeds (M FCFA)
Net loss if it fails (M FCFA)

outputs.label: Worst-case loss as share of reserves

notes.t: ⚠️ The worst case exceeds reserves — positive EV or not, this bet could sink you. Stage it, insure it, or find partners.
✓ Positive EV and survivable. Now pre-mortem it and check the probability against a reference class.
Negative or zero EV — what would need to be true for this to be worth it?

modules.t: Day 2 — Influence, Executive Communication & Leading Leaders
modules.d: Influencing without authority, communicating to boards, and building the leadership bench beneath you.
modules.body:
Influence at the top is mostly lateral and upward

Senior leaders discover that formal authority matters less as they rise. Peers run their own divisions, boards hold ultimate authority, partners and regulators are outside the hierarchy. Executive effectiveness depends on influence without authority: building agreement among people who do not have to agree with you.

The currencies of influence

Allan Cohen and David Bradford's model treats influence as exchange: understand what the other person values — their "currencies" — and what you can offer. Currencies include resources, information, visibility, support for their goals, recognition, relationship, and alignment with their values or mission. Influence fails when executives offer only what they value. Robert Cialdini's research identifies durable principles of persuasion — reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity and unity (shared identity). Used ethically, they help good ideas get heard; used manipulatively, they destroy trust once discovered.

Stakeholder mapping at the executive level

Before any major initiative, map the stakeholders whose support or resistance will decide it: their interests, influence, current position, and what would move them. Meet the most influential sceptics before the decision meeting. Executive decisions are rarely made in the meeting; they are made in the conversations beforehand. A proposal that surprises key stakeholders in a board meeting usually fails.

Communicating to boards and senior audiences

Boards and executive committees have limited time and broad responsibilities. Barbara Minto's pyramid principle structures communication for them: lead with the answer or recommendation, then the key supporting arguments, then the supporting data. This reverses the academic habit of building up to a conclusion. A strong board paper states what decision is needed, the recommendation, the reasons, the risks and mitigations, the alternatives considered, and what success will look like — ideally on one or two pages, with detail in appendices.

Data storytelling. Executives need insight, not data dumps. One chart that shows the critical trend, clearly labelled, with a headline stating the conclusion ("Applications from employer partners have tripled since 2024") is worth more than ten tables. Pair numbers with a concrete example that makes them human.

Leading leaders: the pipeline transitions

Ram Charan, Stephen Drotter and James Noel's Leadership Pipeline describes the transitions leaders must make as they rise: from managing self to managing others, to managing managers, to managing a function, to a business, to a group, to an enterprise. At each transition, leaders must change three things: skills, time application and work values — what they believe is important work. The most common failure: a senior leader who still values the work they used to do, and so micromanages managers and starves strategic work of time.

Leading managers means developing their leadership, not doing their jobs: selecting and developing first-line leaders, holding them accountable for leading (not just producing), coaching them through their own transitions, and building cross-team collaboration.

Building the bench: succession and development

An executive's legacy is measured partly by the strength of the leaders they leave behind. Practical steps: identify critical roles and potential successors; distinguish readiness now from potential; give high-potential leaders stretch assignments with support; use the 70-20-10 guide (most development comes from challenging experience, some from relationships and feedback, a smaller part from formal learning); and review the bench regularly with the same seriousness as financial results.

Managing up and working with boards

Effective executives understand their board's or superior's priorities, pressures and preferred communication style; raise problems early with options; never let them be surprised by bad news from someone else; and respect the boundary between governance (board) and management (executive). Disagreements are voiced clearly in private and decisions, once made, are supported in public — unless they cross an ethical line.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my board communication coach. I will paste a draft board paper or describe a proposal. Rewrite it using the pyramid principle: decision required, recommendation, three key reasons, risks and mitigations, alternatives considered, success measures — within one page. Then role-play the two most sceptical board members, asking the hardest questions, and evaluate my answers.

📚 Glossary

  • Influence without authority: gaining agreement from people outside your control
  • Currencies: what stakeholders value and can be exchanged
  • Pyramid principle: communicate the answer first, then supporting logic
  • Leadership pipeline: the series of leadership transitions requiring new skills, time use and values
  • 70-20-10: development mostly through experience, then relationships, then formal learning

📖 References

  • Cohen, A. & Bradford, D. Influence Without Authority.
  • Cialdini, R. (2021). Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion (new and expanded).
  • Minto, B. The Pyramid Principle.
  • Charan, R., Drotter, S. & Noel, J. (2011). The Leadership Pipeline.
  • Center for Creative Leadership — 70-20-10 framework.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian COO needs IT's director, a peer, to prioritise her project. She offers extra budget, but the IT director mostly cares about recognition with the board. Using Cohen and Bradford, what should she do?
opts: Raise the budget offer, since resources are the most persuasive currency for any division head
Use scarcity by telling him the funding window closes on Friday unless he agrees right away
Offer currencies the IT director values, such as co-presenting the results to the board
Escalate to the CEO so that formal authority settles the priority conflict between the two units
quiz.x: Influence fails when executives offer only what they value. Escalation (runner-up) may work once but spends goodwill and ignores the exchange model.

quiz.q: A US health system CFO will present a major investment at Thursday's board meeting. Two influential directors are known sceptics. What does the module advise?
opts: Meet the two sceptics individually before Thursday to understand and address their concerns
Ask the chair to limit questions on Thursday so the discussion stays focused on the main numbers
Present the strongest data on Thursday so that the sceptics are persuaded in front of their peers
Postpone the item until the sceptics rotate off the board so the vote is more likely to pass
quiz.x: Executive decisions are made in the conversations beforehand; proposals that surprise key stakeholders usually fail. Strong data on the day (runner-up) still surprises the sceptics.

quiz.q: A Nigerian director drafts a board paper that opens with history, then market analysis, then options, and ends with her recommendation on page 9. Applying Minto's pyramid principle, she should:
opts: Add an executive summary at the end restating the recommendation for directors who skim
Keep the order but shorten each section, so the board reaches the recommendation sooner
Move the options to the front so the board feels it is choosing rather than being told what to do
Lead with the decision needed and recommendation, then key reasons, with detail in appendices
quiz.x: The pyramid principle puts the answer first, then supporting arguments, then data. Shortening (runner-up) keeps the academic build-up that boards find hard to use.

quiz.q: A Kenyan charity's annual review slide shows ten tables of application data. Which revision best follows the module's data storytelling advice?
opts: Move the tables to an appendix and replace them with a bulleted list of the top ten statistics
One labelled chart headlined 'Partner applications tripled since 2024', plus one applicant's story
Convert all ten tables to colourful charts so that the board can scan each one of them more quickly
Keep the tables but highlight the key cells in bold so that board members know where to look
quiz.x: Executives need insight: one clear chart with a conclusion headline, paired with a human example. Ten charts (runner-up) are still a data dump.

quiz.q: A newly promoted Yaoundé division head still reviews every sales proposal his managers write and has little time for strategy. Using the Leadership Pipeline, what is the core problem?
opts: His managers are underperforming and he is right to check their work until results improve
He lacks the technical sales skill needed at division level and should attend advanced training
He has not shifted his work values, time application and skills to the new level of leadership
He has too many direct reports and should restructure to reduce his span of control first
quiz.x: The most common pipeline failure is a leader who still values the work they used to do. Restructuring (runner-up) does not change what he believes is important work.

quiz.q: A Ghanaian bank's CEO wants to strengthen succession for the CFO role. She has a $50,000 development budget for a high-potential manager. Using 70-20-10, which allocation fits best?
opts: Mainly external coaching, because relationships matter more than experience at senior levels
Equal thirds across courses, mentoring and assignments so that no development channel is neglected
Most of it on an executive MBA, with mentoring and a short project as secondary activities
A supported stretch assignment as the main lever, plus mentoring and feedback, with some formal courses
quiz.x: 70-20-10 says most development comes from challenging experience, some from relationships and feedback, less from formal learning. Equal thirds (runner-up) under-weights experience.

quiz.q: An executive in Lagos disagrees strongly with a board decision to enter a new market, which raises no ethical issues. What does the module say she should do after the decision is made?
opts: Continue arguing against it in management meetings so the board hears that staff share her doubts
Support the decision publicly, having voiced her disagreement clearly in private beforehand
Resign, since leading a strategy she disagrees with would compromise her professional integrity
Delay implementation quietly until early data proves whether her concerns were justified
quiz.x: Disagree clearly in private, support in public, unless an ethical line is crossed. Quiet delay (runner-up) undermines governance and trust.

quiz.q: A sales director plans to tell a hesitant client: 'Only three slots remain at this price' when twenty slots are actually available. Per Cialdini and the module, what is the issue?
opts: It is manipulative use of scarcity, which destroys trust once the client discovers the truth
None; scarcity is a well-documented principle and every sales team uses it to close deals
The principle is fine but should be paired with reciprocity, such as offering a free gift first
Scarcity works poorly with clients, so the director should use social proof instead
quiz.x: Cialdini's principles help good ideas get heard when used ethically; false scarcity is manipulation and destroys trust once discovered. Switching principles (runner-up) misses the honesty problem.

quiz.q: A CEO in Douala learns that a key project is three months late. The board chair has not heard yet. The CEO plans to wait until next quarter's report. What does the module advise?
opts: Wait for the report, since raising problems early can make the board micromanage operations
Ask the project manager to brief the chair directly so the CEO stays above operational detail
Fix the delay first and report it to the chair if the recovery plan fails by the end of the quarter
Inform the chair early with options, so the board never hears bad news from someone else
quiz.x: Raise problems early with options and never let superiors be surprised by bad news from others. Fixing first (runner-up) risks exactly that surprise.

quiz.q: A Togolese ministry's directors resist a reform led by a new secretary-general. Cohen and Bradford would ask what the directors value. Which first step best applies stakeholder mapping?
opts: Map each director's interests, influence, current position and what would move them
Identify the most resistant director and replace him to signal that opposition will not be tolerated
Hold a large town-hall meeting to explain the reform's benefits to all ministry staff together
Issue a circular reminding directors that the reform is mandatory under the minister's authority
quiz.x: Mapping interests, influence, position and what would move each stakeholder comes before a major initiative. A town hall (runner-up) communicates broadly but does not address individual currencies.

facts.t: Cialdini's principles: reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity, unity.
facts.more: Unity — shared identity — was added in the 2021 expanded edition. Used manipulatively, all of them destroy trust once discovered.

facts.t: Development mostly from experience, then relationships, then formal learning.
facts.more: A guideline from the Center for Creative Leadership — stretch assignments with support do most of the work.

facts.t: Minto's pyramid principle for boards.
facts.more: Lead with the recommendation, then the key arguments, then the data — the reverse of the academic build-up.

facts.t: At each pipeline transition: skills, time application, work values.
facts.more: The classic failure is a senior leader who still values their old work and micromanages managers.

Recommendation
Three key reasons
Risks and mitigations
Alternatives considered
What success will look like
Appendices with detailed data
labs.tip: Decision → answer → why → what could go wrong → what else → how we'll know → detail.

labs.title: Which influence principle is in play?
labs.intro: Match each tactic to the Cialdini principle it uses.
pairs: Reciprocity
You lend your analyst to a peer's urgent project before asking for budget support
Commitment & consistency
You get the CFO to agree the diagnosis in writing before proposing the fix

Scarcity

plaibox.title: Simulation: the restructuring proposal
plaibox.intro: You're a director at a Yaoundé health NGO proposing to merge two departments. 2 = best, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.

steps.s: Two weeks before the board. The finance director, a respected sceptic, hasn't seen the plan.
o: Let the board meeting be the first time she sees it
Surprising key stakeholders in the meeting usually kills a proposal.
Meet her privately to learn her concerns and values
Right — decisions are made in the conversations before the meeting.
Email her the full 30-page plan to read beforehand
Informative, but it doesn't uncover her currencies or concerns.

steps.s: She worries the merger hides cost overruns. What do you offer?
o: Monthly cost reporting she co-designs
Trades a currency she values — information and control — without diluting the plan.
Stress how strongly the CEO supports it
Leaning on authority to silence a concern breeds resistance.
Promise there will be no overruns
An assurance you can't guarantee — credibility risk later.

steps.s: How do you open the board paper?
o: Background and history of both departments
Context matters but belongs later; boards want the answer first.
The decision needed and your recommendation
Pyramid principle: answer first, then reasons and data.
A data table of five years of departmental costs
A data dump without a headline loses a time-poor board.

steps.s: The board approves a version you think is weaker. A manager asks your view.
o: Say you disagreed and now support the decision
Disagree in private, support in public — unless it crosses an ethical line.
Tell them openly that the board got it wrong
Undermines governance and the decision's chance of success.
Avoid the question and move to the next item
Not harmful, but leaves ambiguity about commitment.

plaibox.win: Executive-grade influence — you pre-wired stakeholders, traded real currencies and respected governance.
plaibox.lose: Revisit: map stakeholders early, offer what they value, lead with the answer, and support decisions once made.

modules.d: Redesigning operating models, governing AI responsibly, and leading change at scale.
modules.body:
Transformation is not a bigger project

A transformation changes how the organisation creates value — its operating model, culture and capabilities — not just a system or a structure. Research and practitioner surveys have repeatedly found that most large transformations fall short of their goals, usually not because the design was wrong, but because leaders underestimated the human, cultural and capability work. Executives who treat transformation as a technical programme managed by a project office tend to fail; those who lead it personally and visibly tend to succeed.

The operating model

An operating model describes how the organisation delivers its strategy: processes (how work flows), organisation (structure, roles, decision rights), people (capabilities, culture, incentives), technology and data, location, and governance and performance management. Redesign starts from the strategy's "how to win" choices and asks which capabilities must be strengthened, which are no longer needed, and how the parts must change together. Changing structure alone — the most common executive move — rarely changes performance, because processes, incentives and behaviours stay the same.

Leading change at scale

John Kotter's eight steps remain a practical checklist: create a sense of urgency grounded in real data; build a guiding coalition of credible leaders; form a clear vision and strategy; communicate it far more than seems necessary; remove obstacles — including leaders who resist; generate short-term wins that prove the change works; sustain acceleration without declaring victory too soon; and anchor the change in culture through promotion, hiring and stories. Kotter's research found that skipping steps creates an illusion of speed and rarely produces results.

The productivity J-curve. Major technology adoption often makes performance worse before it gets better: people learn new tools, processes are redesigned and old habits persist. Executives who expect immediate gains often abandon transformations in the dip. Planning for the J-curve — budgeting time, setting realistic milestones and communicating the expected dip — protects the investment.

The business case for AI adoption

A credible AI business case identifies specific use cases tied to strategic priorities, the expected value (time saved, quality improved, revenue created, risk reduced), the full costs (licences, integration, data preparation, training, change management, governance), the risks, and the measures that will show value. The strongest early cases are usually narrow, high-volume and measurable — document processing, customer response drafting, data analysis — rather than broad promises of transformation. Pilots should have clear success criteria and a decision point: scale, adjust or stop.

Executive AI governance

AI governance makes adoption safe and trustworthy. Executives own its foundations: a clear policy for acceptable use; accountability — named owners for each AI system; risk assessment proportional to impact (an AI that drafts internal summaries needs less control than one that influences hiring, credit or medical decisions); data protection and privacy; human oversight for consequential decisions; testing and monitoring for accuracy, bias and drift; transparency with users and clients; and incident response. Recognised frameworks — the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) and the ISO/IEC 42001 AI management system standard — provide structure, and regulations such as the EU AI Act classify systems by risk level. Executives in Africa should also follow national data protection laws and emerging continental guidance.

Culture: the decisive factor

Culture is the pattern of behaviour that is rewarded and tolerated. Executives shape it less through statements than through what they pay attention to, how they react to crises, what they role-model, how they allocate resources, and whom they promote and remove — Edgar Schein's "primary embedding mechanisms". A transformation that preaches experimentation but punishes failure, or promotes leaders who block change, teaches the opposite of its message.

Your personal transformation charter

You leave Day 3 with a one-page charter: the transformation's purpose and diagnosis, the target operating-model changes, the first three short-term wins, the guiding coalition, the AI use cases and governance safeguards, the key risks, the measures of success, and your personal role — what you will do, stop doing and model differently. This charter becomes the agenda for your 90-day coaching sprint.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my transformation architect. I will describe my organisation and the change I need. Help me diagnose the operating-model elements that must change together, map my change plan to Kotter's eight steps, identify three AI use cases with value, cost, risk and governance safeguards, anticipate the J-curve, and draft a one-page personal transformation charter including what I personally must start, stop and model.

📚 Glossary

  • Operating model: how processes, organisation, people, technology, location and governance deliver strategy
  • Guiding coalition: credible leaders who drive the change together
  • J-curve: temporary performance dip during major adoption
  • AI governance: policies, accountability and controls for responsible AI use
  • NIST AI RMF: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage framework for AI risk
  • Embedding mechanisms: leader behaviours that shape culture

📖 References

  • Kotter, J. (1996/2012). Leading Change.
  • Schein, E. Organizational Culture and Leadership.
  • NIST (2023). AI Risk Management Framework 1.0.
  • ISO/IEC 42001:2023 — AI management systems.
  • Brynjolfsson, E., Rock, D. & Syverson, C. — The productivity J-curve.
  • European Union — Artificial Intelligence Act.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian insurer's CEO announces a 'transformation': a new organisation chart with merged departments. Processes, incentives and IT stay the same. What does the module predict?
opts: Performance improves quickly, because clearer reporting lines reduce coordination costs
Performance improves provided the new chart is communicated far more than seems necessary
Performance rarely changes, since processes, incentives and behaviours are left untouched
Performance declines permanently, because restructuring inevitably destroys institutional knowledge
quiz.x: Changing structure alone rarely changes performance because the other operating-model parts stay the same. Communication (runner-up) helps but cannot substitute for changing processes and incentives.

quiz.q: Three months after a US hospital adopts AI-assisted documentation, clinician throughput is down 12%. The board wants to cancel. What concept should the CIO explain, and what should have been done?
opts: Scope creep; reduce the tool's features so clinicians have fewer things to learn at the start
The productivity J-curve; budget time, set realistic milestones and communicate the expected dip
Groupthink; bring in outside clinicians to test whether the tool actually works as promised
Sunk-cost fallacy; cancel now before more money is spent on a tool that is clearly not working for clinicians
quiz.x: Major tech adoption often dips before improving; planning for it protects the investment. Invoking sunk cost (runner-up) assumes failure without checking whether the dip is the expected learning phase.

quiz.q: A Lagos bank must choose its first AI pilot. Which candidate best matches the module's guidance on strong early business cases?
opts: A chatbot for the board to explore strategic scenarios, with no defined success measure
Drafting responses to 8,000 routine customer emails a month, measured by handling time
An enterprise-wide 'AI transformation' covering every department within twelve months
An AI system that makes final credit approval decisions for small business loans
quiz.x: Strong early cases are narrow, high-volume and measurable. Credit decisions (runner-up for value) are high-impact and need heavier governance and oversight first.

quiz.q: A Kenyan HR department wants to use an AI tool to screen job applicants; the communications team uses AI to draft internal newsletters. How should governance differ?
opts: Both need identical controls, because consistent policies are easier to audit and enforce
Neither needs formal governance until a regulator in Kenya issues specific AI hiring rules
The hiring tool needs stronger risk assessment, bias testing and human oversight than the newsletter
The newsletter needs more control, because it reaches every employee in the organisation
quiz.x: Risk assessment should be proportional to impact; tools influencing hiring are consequential. Identical controls (runner-up) either overburden low-risk use or under-protect high-risk use.

quiz.q: A transformation sponsor in Ghana wants to skip Kotter's 'guiding coalition' step to 'move faster' and go straight to communicating the vision. What did Kotter's research find?
opts: Skipping steps creates an illusion of speed and rarely produces results
The coalition step matters mainly in public institutions, where consensus is legally required
Steps can be done in any order, as long as all eight are completed within the first year
Skipping is acceptable if urgency is very high and the CEO personally leads the change
quiz.x: Kotter found skipping steps rarely works. The high-urgency exception (runner-up) sounds plausible but Kotter offers no such exemption; strong urgency is itself only step one.

quiz.q: A Rwandan telecom's risk committee adopts the NIST AI Risk Management Framework to govern its customer-service chatbot. Which list correctly names the framework's four functions?
opts: Plan, Do, Check, Act — applied to every AI system across its full lifecycle in the organisation
Assess, Approve, Deploy, Monitor — the four gates every AI model must pass before release
Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond — the same core functions used for cybersecurity programmes
Govern, Map, Measure, Manage — with governance running through all the other functions
quiz.x: NIST AI RMF 1.0 uses Govern, Map, Measure, Manage. Identify/Protect/Detect/Respond (runner-up) are from the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, a common confusion.

quiz.q: A CEO in Kigali tells staff 'we want experimentation', but last quarter two managers were demoted after failed pilots. Applying Schein, what is the likely result?
opts: Staff learn from the demotions, not the speech, so experimentation will be avoided
Staff will disregard both signals and wait to see what the next annual strategy document says
Staff will experiment, because the CEO's public statement sets clear expectations for everyone
Staff will experiment more carefully, which is the healthy balance the CEO was looking for
quiz.x: Schein's embedding mechanisms — reactions, promotions, removals — shape culture more than statements. 'More careful experimentation' (runner-up) underestimates how strongly punishment teaches avoidance.

quiz.q: A firm operating in the EU and in Senegal is building a CV-screening AI. Which statement about governance is most accurate?
opts: The EU AI Act bans all AI in hiring, so the firm must abandon the tool for its EU operations
ISO/IEC 42001 certification replaces the need to comply with both EU and Senegalese law
Senegalese rules alone apply, because the AI system is developed by the Senegal-based team
The EU AI Act treats employment uses as high-risk, and Senegal's data protection law also applies
quiz.x: The EU AI Act classifies employment-related systems as high-risk, with obligations; national data protection laws also apply. ISO 42001 (runner-up) structures governance but does not replace legal compliance. Details evolve; verify current rules.

quiz.q: An AI pilot in a Douala firm promised to cut invoice processing time by 30%. After eight weeks, it cut time by 9%, with error rates unchanged. What should happen at the pre-agreed decision point?
opts: Scale it anyway, since any improvement justifies rollout once licences have been purchased
Extend the pilot indefinitely so the team can keep gathering data until results improve
Decide to adjust or stop based on the success criteria, rather than drifting into a default rollout
Cancel all AI work, because one underperforming pilot shows AI is unsuitable for the firm
quiz.x: Pilots need clear criteria and a decision point: scale, adjust or stop. Indefinite extension (runner-up) avoids the decision the pilot structure exists to force.

quiz.q: A transformation charter for a Yaoundé hospital lists purpose, operating-model changes, AI safeguards, risks and measures. What does the module say is still missing?
opts: Vendor quotations for each AI system so procurement can begin immediately
The leader's personal role: what they will do, stop doing and model differently
A five-year financial model projecting savings from each operating-model change
A list of every staff member affected, with their new reporting line and job title
quiz.x: The charter includes first wins, the guiding coalition and the leader's personal role. A financial model (runner-up) may support the business case but is not in the charter's core elements.

facts.t: Kotter's model: urgency → coalition → vision → communicate → obstacles → wins → sustain → anchor.
facts.more: Skipping steps creates an illusion of speed and rarely produces results.

facts.t: NIST AI RMF: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage.
facts.more: A voluntary framework for managing AI risk across the lifecycle; Govern runs through all the others.

facts.t: First international AI management-system standard (2023).
facts.more: ISO/IEC 42001 lets organisations run and certify an AI governance system, like ISO 27001 does for information security.

facts.t: EU AI Act risk levels: unacceptable, high, limited, minimal.
facts.more: Obligations scale with risk — hiring, credit and medical uses face the heaviest controls.

plaibox.title: AI business case & J-curve check
plaibox.intro: Build a narrow, measurable case. Include the full costs, not just licences.

inputs.label: Hours saved per person per week (steady state)
One-off setup: integration, data, training, change (FCFA)

notes.t: ⚠️ Run costs exceed value — narrow to higher-volume tasks or renegotiate before piloting.
Payback beyond a year. Remember the J-curve: early months will be worse than steady state.

modules.d: Six executive coaching sessions turning the intensive into measurable results.
modules.body:
Why the 90 days matter more than the 3 days

Executive education produces insight; behaviour change happens afterwards, under pressure, in the real organisation. Without structured follow-through, most intensive learning fades within weeks as old routines reassert themselves. The 90-day coaching sprint exists to convert your transformation charter into results and your personal leadership commitments into habits.

How executive coaching works

Coaching is not consulting (giving answers) or therapy (healing the past). It is a disciplined conversation that helps you think more clearly, decide more deliberately and act more consistently. Sessions use the GROW model popularised by John Whitmore: Goal (what you want from this session and this quarter), Reality (what is actually happening, with evidence), Options (the range of possible actions), and Will (what you commit to do, by when, and how you will know). Good coaches ask more than they tell, challenge assumptions and hold you to your commitments.

The sprint structure

  • Session 1 (week 1–2) — Contracting and baseline. Confirm the charter, agree success measures for the 90 days, identify stakeholders who will observe your change, and set the coaching agreement: confidentiality, cadence, preparation expectations.
  • Session 2 (week 3–4) — First wins. Review progress on the first short-term wins; address early resistance; refine stakeholder engagement.
  • Session 3 (week 5–6) — Leadership behaviours. Focus on the personal behaviours you committed to change; review observer feedback using feedforward.
  • Session 4 (week 7–8) — Obstacles and decisions. Work through the hardest decision or relationship blocking progress — often a peer, a resistant leader or a resource trade-off.
  • Session 5 (week 9–10) — Sustaining and scaling. Plan how wins become embedded in processes, measures and promotions; prepare the leaders below you to carry the work.
  • Session 6 (week 11–12) — Review and sponsor debrief. Measure results against the baseline, gather observer feedback, capture lessons, and set the next 90-day agenda. A debrief with your sponsor closes the loop.
Preparation is the multiplier. Executives who arrive with a prepared update — progress on commitments, the issue they most need to think through, and evidence — get far more from each session than those who arrive to "see what comes up". Fifteen minutes of preparation is usually worth more than the session itself.

Stakeholder-centred measurement

Marshall Goldsmith's stakeholder-centred coaching measures change through the people who experience your leadership. You select a small group of stakeholders, tell them the behaviours you are working on, ask them for ongoing suggestions, and later ask them to rate whether you have become more or less effective. This creates both accountability and visible change — and it matters because leadership effectiveness is ultimately judged by others.

Measuring results, not activity

At the start of the sprint, define two kinds of measures. Organisational outcomes linked to your charter — for example, cycle time reduced, adoption rate of a new process, a strategic decision taken, an initiative stopped and resources redeployed. Leadership measures — observer ratings of your target behaviours, engagement indicators in your team, or the number of decisions delegated. Review both at sessions 3 and 6.

When progress stalls

Expect at least one stall. Common causes: overloaded calendars leaving no time for the charter, a key relationship blocking progress, or an unrealistic plan. The coaching response is not to push harder but to diagnose: Is this a priority problem (other things are winning), a capability problem (you or your team lack a skill), a relationship problem, or a design problem (the plan itself is wrong)? Each needs a different response.

After the sprint

Successful executives make the sprint rhythm permanent: a quarterly personal review of priorities and behaviours, continued stakeholder feedback, a coach or peer advisory group, and development of the leaders beneath them using the same tools. The goal is not to need the coach — it is to become a leader who coaches others.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my executive coach using the GROW model. Before we start, ask me for my transformation charter commitments and progress since our last session. Then run one coaching session: clarify my goal for today, probe the reality with evidence, help me generate options without giving me the answer, and end with specific commitments, deadlines and how I will measure them. Challenge me if I am avoiding the hardest issue.

📚 Glossary

  • GROW: Goal, Reality, Options, Will coaching model
  • Contracting: agreeing coaching goals, confidentiality and expectations
  • Stakeholder-centred coaching: measuring change through those who experience the leader's behaviour
  • Sponsor debrief: closing review with the executive's sponsor or board

📖 References

  • Whitmore, J. Coaching for Performance.
  • Goldsmith, M. — Stakeholder Centered Coaching.
  • International Coaching Federation — Core Competencies.
  • Watkins, M. (2013). The First 90 Days.

quiz.q: In her first coaching session, a Nairobi COO says she wants to 'delegate more'. The coach asks what is actually happening now, with evidence. Which GROW stage is the coach in?
opts: Reality, because the coach is probing the current situation using specific evidence
Options, because the coach is preparing to list ways she could delegate more effectively
Goal, because the coach is clarifying exactly what the COO wants to achieve this quarter
Will, because the coach is testing how committed she is to changing her current behaviour
quiz.x: Reality explores what is happening now, with evidence. Goal (runner-up) was the previous step, when she named delegation as the aim.

quiz.q: A US executive arrives at session 3 saying, 'Let's see what comes up.' He has no update or evidence. According to the module, what most limits the session's value?
opts: The confidentiality agreement, which prevents the coach from contacting his stakeholders first
The timing, because session 3 is too early to discuss leadership behaviours meaningfully
His lack of preparation; 15 minutes of preparation is often worth more than the session itself
The coach's model, because GROW works poorly without a written agenda from the coach
quiz.x: Preparation — progress on commitments, the key issue and evidence — is the multiplier. The coach's approach (runner-up) matters, but the module puts the burden of preparation on the executive.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian director asks her coach to tell her exactly how to restructure her team. The coach instead asks questions. Why, according to the module?
opts: The coach lacks restructuring expertise and is avoiding giving advice outside her competence
Coaching helps the leader think and decide more clearly; giving answers would be consulting
Coaching is closer to therapy, so the coach must first explore the director's past experiences
Ethics codes forbid coaches from discussing organisational structure with their clients
quiz.x: Coaching is not consulting (answers) or therapy (past). The therapy option (runner-up) confuses the boundaries the module draws.

quiz.q: Using Goldsmith's stakeholder-centred approach, an executive working on 'listening better' should:
opts: Rate himself monthly on listening and share the scores with his coach as evidence of progress
Keep the goal private so stakeholders' ratings are not biased by knowing what he is working on
Ask HR to run an anonymous 360 survey of all staff at the start and end of the sprint
Tell selected stakeholders the behaviour, ask for ongoing suggestions, and later ask them to rate change
quiz.x: Goldsmith's method involves a small group who know the target behaviour and give ongoing suggestions. A broad anonymous 360 (runner-up) measures but lacks the visible accountability loop.

quiz.q: A Ghanaian CEO's sprint measures are: 'six coaching sessions attended' and 'charter shared with team'. What does the module recommend instead?
opts: Financial measures alone, since the sponsor ultimately cares about revenue and cost
Keep these, because attendance and sharing are objective and easy to verify for the sponsor
A single measure: the CEO's own satisfaction rating with the coaching at the end of the sprint
Outcome measures such as cycle time reduced or an initiative stopped, plus observer behaviour ratings
quiz.x: Measure results, not activity: organisational outcomes and leadership behaviour ratings. Financial-only measures (runner-up) miss the leadership behaviour dimension.

quiz.q: By week 6, a Lagos executive has made no progress on her charter. Her calendar is full of operational meetings. Using the module's stall diagnosis, this is most likely:
opts: A design problem; the charter is wrong and should be rewritten from scratch this week
A capability problem; she needs training in the skills the charter requires before continuing
A priority problem; other work is winning, so time for the charter must be protected
A relationship problem; a peer must be blocking her, so the coach should mediate
quiz.x: A full calendar crowding out the charter signals a priority problem. A design problem (runner-up) requires evidence that the plan itself is wrong, not just neglected.

quiz.q: At which sessions does the module say both kinds of measures should be reviewed, and what closes the sprint?
opts: Sessions 3 and 6; a debrief with the sponsor closes the loop
Session 1 and session 6; an external audit of the charter closes the sprint
Sessions 2 and 4; a written self-assessment by the executive closes the sprint
Every session; a celebration event with the executive's team closes the sprint
quiz.x: Measures are reviewed at sessions 3 and 6, and a sponsor debrief closes the loop. Reviewing at every session (runner-up) is not the module's structure.

quiz.q: In session 4, a Douala executive admits the real blocker is a resistant fellow director. What does the module suggest this session is designed for?
opts: Collecting observer feedback on behaviours using feedforward from the executive's team
Working through the hardest decision or relationship blocking progress, such as a resistant peer
Celebrating first wins to rebuild momentum before tackling difficult relationships later
Planning how wins become embedded in processes, measures and promotion decisions
quiz.x: Session 4 targets obstacles and decisions. Embedding wins (runner-up) is session 5's job, after blockers are addressed.

quiz.q: After the 90 days, a Kenyan executive asks how to keep the gains. Which plan best matches the module?
opts: Ask HR to add her charter goals to the annual appraisal and review them once a year
Quarterly personal reviews, ongoing stakeholder feedback, a peer group, and coaching her own leaders
Stop formal reflection to avoid over-analysis and rely on instinct now that habits are formed
Book another 90-day sprint immediately, since progress fades without a coach present
quiz.x: The goal is to not need the coach but to become a leader who coaches others. Repeating sprints (runner-up) keeps dependence on the coach.

quiz.q: In session 1, a coach and a Yaoundé CEO agree on confidentiality, cadence and preparation expectations. Which other step belongs in this session according to the module?
opts: Working through the hardest relationship that is blocking the charter's progress
Reviewing the first short-term wins and addressing early resistance from middle managers
Measuring results against the baseline and capturing lessons for the next quarter
Confirming the charter, agreeing 90-day success measures and naming observer stakeholders
quiz.x: Session 1 is contracting and baseline: confirm charter, measures, stakeholders, agreement. First wins (runner-up) are session 2.

facts.t: Goal, Reality, Options, Will — the coaching session structure.
facts.more: Popularised by John Whitmore. Good coaches ask more than they tell and hold you to the ‘Will’ commitments.

facts.t: Across 12 weeks: contract → wins → behaviours → obstacles → sustain → review.
facts.more: Measures are reviewed at sessions 3 and 6; a sponsor debrief closes the loop.

facts.t: Preparation before each session — often worth more than the session.
facts.more: Bring progress on commitments, the one issue you most need to think through, and evidence.

facts.t: Organisational outcomes and leadership behaviour ratings.
facts.more: Track results, not activity — e.g. cycle time cut, decisions delegated, observer ratings of target behaviours.

labs.title: Diagnose the stall
labs.intro: Week 6 progress has stalled. Which kind of problem is each symptom?
items: Your calendar has no time left for charter work
Urgent operational fires win every week
Your team can't yet build the data dashboards the plan needs
You struggle to give direct feedback to senior managers
A peer director quietly blocks resource transfers
The finance head won't attend charter meetings
The plan assumed a budget that was never approved
Milestones assumed results in month one, ignoring the J-curve
labs.tip: Don't push harder — diagnose. Each cause needs a different response.

labs.title: The 90-day sprint
steps: Contracting and baseline measures
Review first short-term wins
Leadership behaviours and feedforward
Work the hardest blocking decision or relationship
Plan how wins get embedded and scaled
Measure against baseline and sponsor debrief
labs.tip: Set up → early wins → you → obstacles → sustain → review.

plaibox.title: Simulation: your coaching sprint
plaibox.intro: You're a ministry director in Yaoundé three weeks into your sprint. 2 = best, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.

steps.s: Session 2 is tomorrow. You've had a hectic week.
o: Arrive and see what comes up, to stay open-minded
Unprepared sessions waste the multiplier — the coach can only work with what you bring.
Take 15 minutes to note progress, key issue, evidence
Preparation is the multiplier.
Ask to postpone until things calm down at work
Sometimes needed, but things rarely calm down; rhythm matters.

steps.s: Your coach asks about your goal to delegate more. You start explaining why your team isn't ready.
o: Let the coach agree that the team is not ready yet
Comfortable, but avoids testing your assumption.
Ask which two-way-door decisions could go to the team
Turns Reality into Options — and tests the assumption with low risk.
Drop the delegation goal from the coaching charter
Abandons the very behaviour change the sprint exists for.

steps.s: How will you know your leadership behaviour has changed?
o: Your own sense of progress, noted in a weekly journal
Leadership is judged by others; self-rating is unreliable.
Ask chosen stakeholders for suggestions, then ratings
Stakeholder-centred measurement creates accountability and visible change.
Track how many hours a week you spend in meetings
An activity proxy, not evidence of effectiveness.

steps.s: Week 12. Results are mixed: one win, one stalled initiative.
o: Report only the win to your sponsor to keep momentum
Hides learning and erodes trust.
Present both against baseline, with lessons and next steps
Honest review turns the sprint into a permanent rhythm.
Extend the sprint by a month until both succeed
May help, but skips the review and decision point.

plaibox.win: You coached like an executive — prepared, tested your assumptions, measured through others and reviewed honestly.
plaibox.lose: Revisit the sprint: prepare, use GROW to explore options, measure via stakeholders, and review against baseline.
